format: General Training: TRUE/FALSE/NOT GIVEN
passage:
Allotments: A Growing Interest

A  Across Britain, on the edges of towns and squeezed between railway lines and housing estates, lie patchworks of small rectangular gardens, each with its own shed, compost heap and rows of vegetables. These are allotments: plots of land, usually owned by the local council, which individuals rent for a modest annual fee in order to grow their own food. For much of the late twentieth century, allotments were regarded as an old-fashioned pastime, associated mainly with retired men. Today they are in such demand that many councils have long waiting lists.

B  The tradition has deep roots. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, as common land was enclosed and rural workers lost access to land on which to grow food, small plots were provided to help poor families feed themselves. In 1908, a law required local councils in England and Wales to provide allotments where there was sufficient demand, an obligation that still exists today. A traditional plot measures ten 'poles', an old unit of measurement, which is roughly 250 square metres, or about the size of a tennis court.

C  Allotments reached their peak during the two world wars, when food shortages made home-grown vegetables essential. During the Second World War, a government campaign urged people to 'Dig for Victory', and parks, playing fields and even the edges of railway lines were turned over to food production. By the end of the war there were more than a million allotments in Britain. In the decades that followed, however, as food became cheaper and more plentiful and many people moved to homes with gardens, demand fell sharply, and many sites were sold for housing.

D  Interest began to revive in the early twenty-first century, driven by concerns about food quality, the environment and the cost of living, as well as by television programmes celebrating home cooking. The profile of allotment holders has also changed: younger people, families and women now make up a much larger share than in the past. Because demand has grown faster than the supply of land, some councils have divided traditional plots in half, allowing more people to have a share, and some waiting lists stretch to several years.

E  Supporters argue that the benefits go well beyond cheap vegetables. Working outdoors provides regular physical exercise, and many plot holders describe their allotment as a place where they can forget the pressures of work. Several studies have linked gardening with improvements in mood and well-being. Allotment sites also bring together people of different ages and backgrounds, who share advice, seeds and surplus produce. Some doctors have even begun to recommend gardening to patients as part of so-called 'social prescribing'.

F  Allotments are not without their challenges. Plots demand regular attention, especially in summer, and new tenants sometimes underestimate the work involved, abandoning their plots after a single season. Most sites have rules requiring a certain proportion of each plot to be cultivated, and tenants who neglect their land may be asked to leave. Nevertheless, for those prepared to commit the time, an allotment offers something increasingly rare in modern life: a direct connection with the seasons and with the source of their food.

Northway Engineering: First Aid at Work Training

A  Course overview. The company is looking for volunteers to train as workplace first aiders. The three-day course, run by an approved external provider, covers the treatment of injuries such as burns, cuts and broken bones, as well as how to respond to someone who has collapsed.

B  Dates and location. The next course will run from 12 to 14 May in Training Room 2 at our main site. Sessions start at 9.00 a.m. and finish at 4.30 p.m., with lunch provided.

C  Who can apply. Any permanent employee may apply, but priority will be given to staff on the night shift and at the Eastfield warehouse, where we currently have fewer qualified first aiders. Applicants should be comfortable with practical activities, including kneeling on the floor.

D  Assessment. Participants are assessed throughout the course through practical tasks, and there is a short written test at the end. Those who pass receive a certificate valid for three years. A one-day refresher course must be completed before the certificate expires.

E  Benefits. Qualified first aiders receive an additional payment of £250 per year. Time spent on the course counts as normal working hours.

format: General Training: TRUE/FALSE/NOT GIVEN
passage:
Working Less, Achieving More? The Four-Day Week

A  For most of the twentieth century, the standard working week in industrialised countries shrank steadily. In the early 1900s, factory employees commonly worked six days a week; by the middle of the century, the five-day, forty-hour week had become the norm in many countries. Since then, however, the length of the standard week has barely changed, even as technology has transformed the nature of work. In recent years, a growing number of employers and campaigners have asked whether the next step should be a four-day week.

B  It is important to distinguish between two very different ideas that are sometimes given the same name. A 'compressed' week involves working the same total number of hours over four days, for example four ten-hour days. A reduced-hours week, by contrast, cuts the total working time, typically to around thirty-two hours, while maintaining full pay. Advocates of the latter often refer to the '100-80-100' model: employees receive 100 per cent of their pay for 80 per cent of their time, in return for a commitment to maintain 100 per cent of their productivity.

C  Some of the most widely cited evidence comes from Iceland, where trials involving around 2,500 public-sector workers took place between 2015 and 2019. Working hours were reduced from forty to thirty-five or thirty-six per week, without any reduction in pay. According to researchers who analysed the results, productivity and service provision remained the same or improved in the majority of workplaces, while workers reported lower stress and a better balance between work and home life. Following the trials, unions negotiated agreements giving many Icelandic workers the right to request shorter hours.

D  In 2022, a six-month pilot involving 61 companies and almost 3,000 employees took place in the United Kingdom. The organisations ranged from small marketing agencies to a fish and chip shop. At the end of the trial, 56 of the companies chose to continue with the four-day week, 18 of them on a permanent basis. Employees reported less burnout and fewer sick days, and among the companies that provided financial data, revenue stayed broadly the same over the trial period. Many firms found that the change forced them to cut unnecessary meetings and to reorganise tasks more efficiently.

E  Sceptics, however, point to several limitations. The companies taking part in such trials had volunteered, and are likely to have been those most confident that a shorter week would suit them. Six months may be too short a period to reveal long-term effects. Moreover, the model is far easier to apply in office-based work, where output can be measured in tasks completed, than in sectors such as healthcare, education or retail, where staff need to be present for fixed periods. In these areas, reducing hours without reducing pay may simply require employing more people, which raises costs.

F  The debate is therefore likely to continue for some time. It seems unlikely that a single model will suit every industry, and the most successful examples so far have involved careful planning and the active involvement of employees in redesigning their work. What the trials have demonstrated, at the very least, is that the number of hours spent at work is not always a reliable measure of what is achieved there.

Westbrook Public Library: Our Services

A  Borrowing. Members can borrow up to 12 items at a time, including books, DVDs and audiobooks. Items are loaned for three weeks and can be renewed twice online, by phone or in person, unless another member has reserved them.

B  Membership. Membership is free for everyone who lives, works or studies in the area. To join, bring a document showing your current address. Children under 16 need a parent or guardian to sign the form.

C  Study spaces. Quiet study desks are available on the first floor on a first-come, first-served basis. Group study rooms for up to six people can be booked for a maximum of two hours per day.

Items cannot be renewed if someone has reserved them.
Members may borrow 12 books and 12 DVDs at once.
Renewals can only be made in person at the library.
answer: Items cannot be renewed if someone has reserved them.
explanation: A「can be renewed twice ... unless another member has reserved them」。合計12点まで、更新は オンライン・電話でも できる。

passage:
Westbrook Public Library: Our Services

A  Borrowing. Members can borrow up to 12 items at a time, including books, DVDs and audiobooks. Items are loaned for three weeks and can be renewed twice online, by phone or in person, unless another member has reserved them.

B  Membership. Membership is free for everyone who lives, works or studies in the area. To join, bring a document showing your current address. Children under 16 need a parent or guardian to sign the form.

C  Study spaces. Quiet study desks are available on the first floor on a first-come, first-served basis. Group study rooms for up to six people can be booked for a maximum of two hours per day.

D  Computers and printing. Free computer use is available for up to one hour a day. Printing costs 10p per black-and-white page and 50p per colour page. Staff can help with basic computer skills on Tuesday mornings.

E  Events. Our weekly events include story time for under-5s on Friday mornings and a reading group for adults on the last Thursday of each month. Events are free, but places for the reading group should be booked.
question:
Complete the sentence below. Choose ONE WORD ONLY from the passage for the answer.

To join the library, people must bring a document showing their current ______.
explanation: B「bring a document showing your current address」。

passage:
Job Description: Assistant Store Manager, GreenLeaf Garden Centres

A  Job purpose. To support the Store Manager in running a busy garden centre, ensuring that customers receive excellent service and that the store meets its sales targets. You will take charge of the store in the manager's absence.

B  Main responsibilities. Supervising a team of up to 20 staff, including seasonal workers; preparing weekly staff rotas; monitoring stock levels and placing orders with suppliers; ensuring that plants are properly cared for and displayed; and handling customer complaints that cannot be resolved by other staff.

C  Requirements. At least two years' supervisory experience in a retail environment is essential. A knowledge of plants and gardening is desirable but not essential. A full driving licence is required, as the role involves occasional travel to other branches.

D  Working hours. 40 hours per week, including alternate weekends. Additional hours may be required during the busy spring season, for which overtime is paid.

E  Benefits. Staff receive a 20% discount on all products, free parking and access to the company's training programme, which can lead to a recognised management qualification.
question:
Does the following statement agree with the information given in the passage? Choose TRUE if the statement agrees with the information, FALSE if the statement contradicts the information, or NOT GIVEN if there is no information on this.

The assistant manager will run the store when the manager is not there.
explanation: A「You will take charge of the store in the manager's absence」。TRUE。
